case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old male was referred for evaluation of a painless right lower-eyelid lesion noted during routine glaucoma follow-up. The lesion had been present for 3 years with slow, gradual enlargement. The patient denied any associated symptoms. He was a former smoker and had no history of skin cancer or immunosuppression. The remainder of his medical history was noncontributory. Inspection of the right lower eyelid revealed a cystic-appearing nodule that transilluminated and had a few overlying telangiectasias. The cystic portion was continuous with a deeper, smooth subcutaneous component that was well defined, firm, and nonmobile, with a total lesion length of 1 cm (Figure 1A). There was no madarosis, eyelid margin effacement or preauricular lymphadenopathy. Although no overt features of malignancy were present, the deeper component was atypical for a hidrocystoma and an excisional biopsy was performed. Histopathologic evaluation showed a neoplasm composed of low-grade round nuclei growing in a micropapillary pattern within pools of extracellular mucin (Figure 1B). There was tumor present at the margin. Immunostains were positive for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor. Variable staining for INSM1, a sensitive nuclear stain for neuroendocrine differentiation, and focal staining for synaptophysin, another neuroendocrine marker, were also seen. This immunophenotype is consistent with a primary tumor derived from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma or a metastatic mucinous carcinoma of breast origin.
case_info.caption: Cystic-appearing subcutaneous nodule with a few overlying telangiectasias measuring approximately 1 cm identified just below the eyelash line (A). Histopathology revealed micropapillae of tumor cells floating within pools of mucin (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification × 10) (B).
case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

This immunophenotype is consistent with a primary tumor derived from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma or a metastatic mucinous carcinoma of breast origin.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

case_info.explanation: Mucinous carcinoma of the eyelid Cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is a rare, low-grade malignant neoplasm of the sweat glands. It often presents as a slow-growing asymptomatic nodule, most commonly on the eyelid and the face.1The histogenesis is disputed; while previously thought to be of eccrine origin, recent evidence suggests it demonstrates apocrine-type differentiation.2Particularly on the eyelid, it may arise from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma. Due to its low incidence, literature on this disease is limited. Most commonly, cutaneous mucinous carcinoma presents as a primary lesion but 5% to 6% are metastatic in origin.1,3In metastatic disease, common sites of tumor origin include the breast and gastrointestinal tract. Thus, once a diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma is made, it is critical to evaluate for metastatic disease with full-body imaging (choice D).4,5After metastatic workup is completed, a treatment plan can be determined. In this case, wide local resection (choice A) is not the preferred next step as systemic disease should first be ruled out. Similarly, excision with frozen sections (choice B) would not be recommended before evaluating for metastatic disease. Mohs surgery (choice C) would also not be preferred until a systemic workup is complete. After ruling out systemic disease, treatment of mucinous carcinoma is complete excision. Evidence suggests a lower rate of recurrence in patients undergoing excision with frozen section margins or Mohs surgery than wide local excision, as the extent of the tumor can be difficult to gauge clinically due to its infiltrative nature and the grossly normal appearance and texture of involved tissues.6 The incidence of distant metastasis in cutaneous mucinous carcinoma is significantly higher in eyelid tumors than other primary anatomic sites.1,3In addition, eyelid involvement has been shown to have higher rates of recurrence of up to 30% to 40%.6-8In a large population-based study of 411 cases, there were 10 deaths reported due to primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma; however, only 1 eyelid tumor was associated with death.3Because of the high recurrence rate and possibly devastating outcomes, patients with primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma should be monitored closely. Given the benign appearance of the tumor, ophthalmologists should take extra care when evaluating eyelid lesions with cystic features to not miss disease with metastatic potential. Fortunately, despite the higher incidence of distant metastasis and recurrence, eyelid tumors have not been found to be associated with worse survival.3 After the initial biopsy confirmed mucinous carcinoma with positive margins, the patient underwent metastatic workup with a computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, which were unrevealing. He then underwent a full-thickness wedge resection of the entire visibly involved area with additional 2-mm margins of normal-appearing tissue medially, laterally, and inferiorly. These specimens were sent for rush permanent pathology. Surprisingly, all the margins returned positive. The patient returned for excision with frozen sections. In total, 22 frozen section specimens were needed to achieve negative margins, leaving a large lower-eyelid defect (Figure 2). The patient ultimately underwent reconstruction and has been disease free since.

[Case]
A 62-year-old male was referred for evaluation of a painless right lower-eyelid lesion noted during routine glaucoma follow-up. The lesion had been present for 3 years with slow, gradual enlargement. The patient denied any associated symptoms. He was a former smoker and had no history of skin cancer or immunosuppression. The remainder of his medical history was noncontributory. Inspection of the right lower eyelid revealed a cystic-appearing nodule that transilluminated and had a few overlying telangiectasias. There was no madarosis, eyelid margin effacement or preauricular lymphadenopathy. Although no overt features of malignancy were present, the deeper component was atypical for a hidrocystoma and an excisional biopsy was performed. There was tumor present at the margin. Immunostains were positive for estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor. Variable staining for INSM1, a sensitive nuclear stain for neuroendocrine differentiation, and focal staining for synaptophysin, another neuroendocrine marker, were also seen. This immunophenotype is consistent with a primary tumor derived from endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma or a metastatic mucinous carcinoma of breast origin.
